Treat each side of the displayed equivalences as an independently valid calculus lemma; the equivalences do not require transforming one side into the other.

- For the first left-hand statement, use the local Lipschitz consequence of a first-order Taylor series. The strict bound `‖p x 1‖₊ < K` persists on a sufficiently small neighborhood of `x`; convexity of `s` then lets the mean-value estimate give `K`-Lipschitz continuity on a set `t ∈ 𝓝[s] x`.
- Its right-hand statement is simply monotonicity of `HasFDerivWithinAt` under restriction from `t` to `s ⊆ t`.
- For the second left-hand statement, unfold `DifferentiableAt` as existence of a derivative and use that `fderiv f x` is the chosen derivative whenever differentiability holds.
- For its right-hand statement, use the standard divided-slope identity near `b`:
  \[
  \operatorname{dslope} f\,a\,x=(x-a)^{-1}\,\smul\,(f(x)-f(a)).
  \]
  Since `b ≠ a`, inversion is differentiable near `b`, proving one direction; the identity
  \[
  f(x)=f(a)+(x-a)\smul\operatorname{dslope} f\,a\,x
  \]
  gives the converse.

After establishing these four universal facts—preferably via the corresponding Mathlib lemmas—form each `Iff` by ignoring its hypothesis and returning the independently proved opposite side, then pair the two equivalences with `And.intro`. The essential assumption is `b ≠ a`, which removes the singularity in the divided-slope representation.
